Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

vignette:
Amina had spent most of her adult life on trains, moving through the rail corridors of the eastern seaboard, working the long shifts that came with being a conductor and managing crowds, delays, and the small emergencies that came with the job. The trauma began years earlier, during a period of political unrest while she was traveling home in Africa, when armed men stopped the vehicle she was in, dragged her out, and held her for hours. She was beaten and burned, and the memory of the smoke around her, the sharp smell of it, and the sight of injuries on bodies nearby has never left her. What she remembers now is not a clear sequence but flashes: a hand reaching, a boot, blood on skin, a wall, smoke turning the air bitter. Even when she tries to tell herself the story from beginning to end, it comes apart in her mind, and she is left with images rather than a narrative she can follow. When she remembers it, she feels as if it is happening right now, not as something past and finished.

In the months and years that followed, Amina began to notice that certain moments could seize her without warning. Complete silence, especially at night, made her stop and listen. If the house was too quiet, she would lie awake waiting for a sound that meant someone was entering, her ears straining for the smallest shift in the dark. A whiff of smoke from a neighbor’s grill, a candle left burning, or even the smell of something singed on the stove could pull her sharply back toward the worst hours of her captivity. Seeing visible injuries on other people, even a scraped arm or a cut hand, had a similar effect; her attention would lock onto wounds as if they were danger signals. Those moments pushed her into habits she believed might keep her safer: she checked her body constantly for signs of injury or threat, ran through worst case scenarios in her mind so she would not be caught unprepared, and smoked more heavily, telling herself it helped her steady her nerves.

The same fragments that came back to her in those moments also shaped the way she now moves through the world. Her memories are mostly pictures, and when one image flashes up, the old fear comes with it. A sudden movement in her husband’s hands across the kitchen or an abrupt gesture from a stranger on the platform can make her stiffen immediately, as if her body has already decided that harm is near. She has become convinced that she must stay alert at all times because danger can arrive in an instant and without warning, and that conviction keeps her from relaxing even in her own home. At work, where the train cars sometimes fall into an unusual hush between announcements, she feels the tension rise in her chest and starts scanning faces, exits, and the condition of passengers’ bodies, watching for injuries, odd movements, or any sign that something is wrong. The more she scans, the less ease she feels, and the less she can settle.

Amina has come to live in a narrowing loop. The more she checks her body, smokes, and rehearses disasters, the more her mind stays fixed on threat, and the more easily the old images break through. When she is on guard, she notices every silence, every smell of smoke, every sudden movement, and each of those moments carries her back toward the same incomplete, overpowering pictures. The memory then arrives with such force that it feels current again, which makes her more frightened of being unprepared and more determined to keep monitoring. Over time, that has left her exhausted and irritable, less present with her husband, and increasingly unable to rest even when the train ride is over and she is home. She has finally sought help because she is tired of living as if the torture could start again at any moment, and because she fears that if she keeps going like this she will never feel safe, or never truly come back to herself.
